While it gives software tips, the framing is about community-level sustainability and the RSE profession's response to workforce instability.
abstract: Loss of key personnel has always been a risk for research software projects. Key members of a team may have to step away due to a change in national or university funding, due to illness or burnout, or because they are simply changing jobs. Today, political and financial changes are putting large numbers of researchers out of work simultaneously, both in the UK and abroad, potentially leaving large amounts of research software abandoned and destabilising necessary digital research infrastructure. We present ten tips to help researchers ensure that the software they have built will continue to be usable after they have left their present job, for any reason. These techniques, methods, and best practices were collectively sourced from researchers from dozens of universities across the globe, and are now being improved upon in a ReSA Task Force. The tips shown here will enable individual researchers and labs to position their work in a way that makes it more sustainable and usable going forward, resulting in a more resilient research software ecosystem.

title: Reimagining Digital Accessibility: From Compliance to Collective Responsibility at King's Digital Lab
reasoning: This is about a cross-cutting software engineering practice (accessibility process integrated into SDLC) applicable to RSE teams generally, with strong community/team dynamics elements.
abstract:
Digital accessibility is often seen as a compliance issue, but King’s Digital Lab’s experience shows it is deeply rooted in human connection, team dynamics, and strategic thinking. We share our current approach to embedding accessibility within research software projects. Informed by years of learning and feedback, the updated process is designed to be both practical and collaborative, ensuring accessibility is actively considered across software development roles and project phases, encouraging shared ownership across disciplines. 
 
In 2023, we formed a dedicated accessibility team involving a designer, engineer, and project manager to lead a procedural shift. The approach builds on lessons learnt from previous efforts and is structured around our Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), supported by shared documentation and visual artefacts, with stages aligned to clearly defined roles and responsibilities. 
 
The process was trialed on active projects to test its usability, refine documentation, and identify areas for improvement within ongoing project workflows. This iterative rollout ensured the approach stayed responsive to real team needs, while encouraging open feedback and continuous refinement. We focused on building a process that promotes engagement, adaptability, and sustained momentum over rigid compliance. 
 
The poster outline key principles and elements that shaped our process, offering RSE teams to reflect on, adapt, or build upon in their own contexts. Our process begins by prioritising accessibility requirements using the MoSCoW method, followed by scoping with the project team. Assessments and fixes are integrated continuously during development. Fixes are documented in GitHub; unresolved issues, tools, and methods are recorded in the accessibility statement when needed. 
 
We welcome feedback, collaboration, and insights from others exploring inclusive, process-based strategies for accessibility in technical and research-focused environments. Our goal is to foster accessible outputs through approaches that are inclusive not just of users, but of the research software teams that create them.

title: Making Software Easy-Build Friendly: Streamlining HPC Software Deployment
reasoning: EasyBuild is a general-purpose HPC software deployment framework that applies across research domains, focusing on packaging, reproducibility, and build automation.
abstract:
Reproducible, maintainable, and scalable software builds are fundamental to high-performance computing (HPC) environments. However, the traditional approach of manually compiling and configuring scientific software is often time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult to replicate across systems. This presentation explores how making software EasyBuild-friendly significantly simplifies the process of deploying complex software stacks on HPC systems.
EasyBuild is an open-source framework that automates the building, installation, and management of scientific software on HPCs. By creating EasyBuild “easyconfigs” and optionally writing custom “easyblocks,” users can define builds declaratively—reducing the need for manual intervention and ensuring consistent results across installations. The session will cover key principles for adapting or packaging software to be EasyBuild-friendly, including proper handling of dependencies, versioning, environment modules, and integration with software stack management tools like Lmod.
Through practical examples, we will demonstrate how to convert manual build processes into automated EasyBuild recipes. We will highlight the benefits for both research software engineers and end-users: faster deployment, simplified software stack maintenance, and improved reproducibility. Attendees will also learn how to contribute back to the EasyBuild ecosystem, making their software accessible to a broader HPC audience.
By adopting EasyBuild in research environments, institutions can reduce redundant work, standardize their software environments, and free up valuable researcher time. This talk aims to empower RSEs to leverage EasyBuild not just as users, but as contributors shaping the future of sustainable HPC software deployment.

title: Making a SPLASH: How digital tools are revolutionising wave overtopping prediction
reasoning: This is a domain-specific tool built for coastal wave overtopping prediction, a specific environmental/oceanographic research application.
abstract:
The SPLASH project   has created an environmental digital twin able to forecast and visualise wave overtopping to support coastal communities in high-risk flooding areas. It provides an excellent example of RSE teams combining user centred design, interactive plotting, machine learning and containerisation to take a scientist’s proof of concept Jupyter notebook to an easy-to-use web dashboard.  
 The SPLASH digital twin uses a random forest machine learning model trained on wind, water level and wave data combined with wave overtopping data from a WireWall sensor. A test scenario is based around the coastal railway in Dawlish, Devon, and a coastal frontage with high social value (recreation and tourism) in Penzance, Cornwall. Overtopping data and forecast conditions are displayed on an interactive dashboard able to display wave overtopping graphs from today up to five days ahead. This dashboard also allows users to adjust the wave, water level and atmospheric features to predict new overtopping scenarios and understand how these variables influence the overtopping hazard. The tool is built using a Plotly Dash frontend and models in scikit-learn.  Up-to-date wave and wind forecast data is obtained from the Met Office through a set cron scripts and the tidal levels are obtained from local predictions. A set of Docker containers are used to run the frontend, backend and downloader making the whole system easy to deploy on a dedicated server, virtual machine or cloud provider. This research shows how integrating machine learning models with digital technologies enables prediction of wave overtopping very efficiently. This digital tool serves as a decision-support system for mitigating coastal hazard, e.g. impact by overtopping waves, benefiting both community policy makers and railway operators with infrastructure in affected regions.

title: Bridging Academia and Industry: An RSE’s Perspective on Commercial Collaboration
reasoning: This talk focuses on the RSE profession itself—specifically the experience of working on commercial collaborations, navigating contracts, politics, and skills required. It's about the RSE role and career, not a specific tool or research domain.
abstract: Research Software Engineers (RSEs) often operate at the intersection of software development and academic inquiry. However, their roles can extend far beyond traditional research boundaries. This presentation explores the unique challenges and insights gained from working as an RSE on a commercial project in partnership with a university. Unlike typical research-focused roles, commercial engagements involve navigating complex contract negotiations, company politics, and differing expectations in project management and delivery. Drawing from a recent experience, I will detail a collaboration where a company initially relied on generative AI to convert mathematical formulas into Python code. When the results fell short, both mathematical insight and computational rigor were needed—prompting the company to seek support from our university. This case study highlights the technical, organizational, and interpersonal skills required of RSEs in commercial settings, as well as the pros and cons of stepping beyond purely research-oriented work.

title: Harnessing the power of AIRR supercomputers for trusted research
reasoning: FRIDGE is a cross-cutting TRE platform built on HPC/AIRR for secure AI research—general-purpose infrastructure serving researchers across domains, not tied to a specific scientific question.
abstract:
How can we use the country's most powerful supercomputers for research on sensitive data while keeping that data secure?

Complex AI models trained on large datasets are having a enormous impact in many research domains. However, training and applying such models requires high performance hardware and specialist accelerators such as GPUs. The new AI Research Resource (AIRR) has greatly expanded the availability of GPU-enabled compute to support large scale AI research in the UK.

Working with sensitive data requires high levels of security to ensure that the data is only accessible by approved researchers, and only for approved research. Trusted Research Environments (TREs) provide secure analysis environments for working safely with sensitive data. However, TREs do not provide the computational power and scaling that is required for the development and application of large models. Conversely, high performance computing (HPC) platforms do not generally support TRE capabilities, and therefore cannot provide sufficient security for working with sensitive data.

In FRIDGE we are building a SATRE and NHS standards compliant, cross-platform TRE on AIRR; unlocking the power of these system for AI-driven research using sensitive data.

In our talk we will discuss,
The unique challenges of creating a secure enclave on a shared resource
How we approach the problem of building a TRE to be transferable between multiple HPC systems, and clouds, using IAC and Kubernetes
How FRIDGE can be used to add new capabilities to existing TREs
Enforcing security through policy as code
How we solve governance, when responsibility is shared between the HPC site and TRE operator
The different TRE architectures we considered, and how we arrived at our choice

title: Observability: A Practical Primer for RSEs
reasoning: Cross-cutting software engineering practice (observability) applicable to RSEs across domains, with general-purpose tools.
abstract:
When you distribute and run your software, do you have a good idea of how it's functioning "in the wild"? Do your users have to manually report back to you when they find a bug - and do you have access to the software state when it occurred? How do you know if your application has enough resources when running on a cluster or the cloud, and at what rate it's processing datasets/jobs?

These questions are some of the motivating use cases underpinning observability, which can broadly be defined as using event-driven data (telemetry) to gain insights into the functioning of both software and infrastructure. Observability is useful for troubleshooting issues on production systems, monitoring performance and security, and for tracking key metrics and events happening within a system.

In this introductory walkthrough, I will introduce observability in the context most often used by RSEs - running software in "batch" mode (e.g. running on a cluster) or "server" mode (long-running applications on cloud or workstations). The three main telemetry types will be introduced - metrics, logs, traces - and I will demonstrate how to capture metrics from Python applications in "batch" mode using Microbench (pypi.org/project/microbench) and in "server" mode using OpenTelemetry (opentelemetry.io) and Prometheus (prometheus.io). I will share resources for capturing logs and traces (for later study, in the interests of time). The emphasis will be on simple, practical examples that RSEs can adopt into their own software with minimal fuss.

title: Record a goose sighting: an introduction to accessibility testing for RSEs
reasoning: Workshop on accessibility testing as a cross-cutting software engineering practice applicable to any research software UI.
abstract:
Research software should be accessible to everyone, including people with disabilities. In many cases, it’s a legal requirement. But how do we know if our software meets accessibility standards?
In this workshop, you will learn how to perform accessibility testing on user interfaces and webpages. Guided by real-world user personas, you will explore a fictional government service for recording goose sightings, and discover how design decisions can create accessibility barriers for some users. You'll then apply what you've learned to search for (and fix!) real accessibility barriers in one of your own projects.
No previous accessibility experience is required, but if you’re comfortable editing a user interface or website, you’ll get more out of the final part of the session.
Our goal is for you to leave with practical and effective inclusive design skills, and the confidence to identify and fix barriers in your own projects.

On the Day Link: https://pad.disroot.org/p/rsecon-a11y-workshop

title: Embedding energy efficiency in computational communities
reasoning: This project surveys multiple computational communities to develop cross-cutting guidance on energy-efficient software practices, benchmarking common libraries like BLAS/LAPACK. It's a general sustainability/efficiency tooling effort applicable across domains, with a community-engagement aspect.
abstract:
The Collaborative Computational Projects (CCPs) are a set of communities funded by CoSeC (https://www.cosec.ac.uk/) that develop and maintain a wide range of scientific software. but without information on energy efficiency, it can be difficult for users and developers to make informed choices about the way they write or use that software. Current understanding is limited, and whilst some communities have started developing guidance on energy efficiency, this is often application specific and time consuming for researchers. Our cross-cutting project aims to generalise existing knowledge of sustainable computing and address common challenges across disciplines by: 
Surveying the CCPs to identify common software libraries, such as BLAS and LAPACK, and challenges to improving energy efficiency,
Benchmarking the performance and carbon intensity of these common software libraries and their alternatives,
Using this information to create best practice guidance to allow RSEs to improve the energy efficiency of their software.

title: How to talk to your documents: An introduction to using natural language to query documents with Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
reasoning: Tutorial on building a general-purpose RAG system using open-source tools, applicable across domains—a cross-cutting software/AI infrastructure topic.
abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are powerful, but they have some well-known limitations particularly when interacting with your own documents. LLMs can hallucinate facts, they don't have access to up-to-date or private information, and they can't always explain where their answers come from. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a way to fix some of these problems by letting the model pull in relevant information from external sources before generating a response. This makes answers more accurate, more current, and easier to verify because the model can cite its sources.
In this session, we'll introduce the basics of how RAG works and then walk through building a complete RAG system from scratch using only open-source tools. We'll use Python, along with libraries like Ollama and LangChain, to show how you can build a local document search system, connect it to an LLM, and get better answers without relying on any external APIs. You’ll learn how to index documents, retrieve them effectively, and generate responses.
We’ll also touch on common RAG limitations, such as the importance of data quality and handling large context sizes. Finally, we’ll look at a few advanced techniques to help improve accuracy and performance. By the end, you’ll have a working understanding of what RAG is, how to implement it using open source tools, and how to build and apply your own RAG powered applications to talk to your own documents.

title: Working with SYCL for a portable and performant library adding reactions to particle codes used in plasma physics.
reasoning: This is about a library built specifically for plasma physics simulations (particle reactions in tokamak exhaust), making it domain-specific research software. SYCL/portability aspects are secondary software-engineering considerations.
abstract: In plasma physics simulations and in particular those of the tokamak exhaust, atomic and molecular reactions can play an important role. These need to be incorporated into various particle codes with many complex reactions and a large number of particles that must be processed, all of these aspects in combination require both flexibility and performance. NESO-Particles is a performance portable framework for building particle codes on meshes (both structured and unstructured) developed at UKAEA, and we have chosen it as a basis for our particle reactions library. NESO-Particles is built on SYCL to provide said performance portability and we inherit this capability in our library. This allows the codes using the library to run on both CPUs and NVidia GPUs on either local machines (such as laptops) or large clusters (such as CSD3 in Cambridge). However, the use of SYCL required certain considerations to be taken into account and posed some design challenges that were overcome. For example we had to consider that all data that is used inside SYCL loops has to be compatible with the SYCL compute device (this is particularly apparent when using GPUs), while ensuring a relatively smooth and flexible installation procedure. This poster showcases various SYCL-based design constraints encountered in this project as well as how Spack was used to manage package dependencies. Additionally, there is also some exploration of the process of open-sourcing the library that has unique configuration and installation considerations owing to its portability via SYCL.

title: Transforming Digital Research Infrastructure for Environmental Science
reasoning: This talk is about delivering Digital Research Infrastructure for environmental science at UKCEH, focusing on team composition, methodologies (Agile, PRINCE2, co-design), and how diverse roles work together. While environmental science is named, the core content is about how to organize teams and practices for DRI delivery — a profession/community topic. There's also a domain-specific angle.
abstract:
Delivering cutting-edge Digital Research Infrastructure (DRI) to support environmental science demands more than just new tools—it requires a fundamental shift in how we work. Much like the proverb “It takes a village to raise a child,” delivering effective DRI demands contributions from a broad community of professionals. Success depends not only on Research Software Engineering (RSE), but also on the combined efforts of experts in DevOps, data science, data management, and design (including Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) and Software Architecture) .

At UKCEH, we’ve embraced a multidimensional approach, drawing on this diverse range of skills and practices. Our large, multi-year DRI projects integrate methodologies such as Agile (Scrum and Kanban), PRINCE2, and co-design. This mix isn't always seamless. We share how these varied approaches and skill sets intersect in practice—what’s worked, where friction has arisen, and how we've adapted to meet the evolving demands of digital environmental science.

title: Enabling Research Software Excellence through RSEng Community Conversations
reasoning: This describes a community-driven conversation series promoting RSE practices in the Global South, focused on community-building and engagement rather than a specific tool or research domain.
abstract:
A six-month-long online community conversation series titled "Enabling Open Science Through Research Code" (https://rse-asia.github.io/RSE_Asia/events.html) was organised jointly by the RSE Asia and RSSE Africa communities from October 2024 to March 2025. Drawing inspiration from CodeRefinery’s (https://coderefinery.org/) training materials, the series was contextualised for the communities in the Global South. Since, in the Global South, the open science movement is comparatively more recognised than the research software engineering (RSE) movement, the message was anchored in the language of open science to broaden reach and engagement among researchers who code.
Each episode featured an open panel discussion on a topic critical to sustainable and reproducible research software practices, such as reproducibility, documentation, and testing. People working in the Asian and African regions or those who had experience working/collaborating with researchers from these regions were invited as panellists. To enhance accessibility,  the sessions were recorded and shared with the communities. Each episode was also accompanied by a summary blog post and a curated resource sheet publicly available on Zenodo.
The impact of the series was visible in community engagement, with RSE Asia’s social media (https://www.linkedin.com/company/rse-asia-association/?viewAsMember=true) engagement rate increasing by 71% during the process. The series also enjoyed popularity with a globally distributed audience across varied time zones.
This poster presents the model that was used for organising this Global South focused community initiative, the strategies that were adopted to increase participation and accessibility, and the types of openly licensed outputs that were co-created. Overall, this series is a testament to how cross-regional collaboration and community-driven efforts can effectively promote research software excellence.

title: Supporting digital research infrastructure with software audits: Help us shape good practice.
reasoning: This workshop is about developing audit practices for research infrastructure, involving policy, profession-wide good practice, and community input to shape UKRI DRI processes. It's about cross-organisation policy and infrastructure rather than a specific tool or domain.
abstract:
Research Software Engineers who attend this workshop will crowdsource priorities and good practice for conducting audits that can support risk-mitigation and funding applications for different types of Compute and Data infrastructures. This work is supported by UKRI, who will be attending the session.

In early 2025, UKRI’s Digital Research Infrastructure (DRI) Programme asked the Software Sustainability Institute to conduct a scoping study on the ‘critical software’ for its compute and data infrastructure investments. We interviewed 6 infrastructures and conducted focus groups with the wider DRI staff and user community.

Findings indicated a range of risks to critical software, as well as the benefits of conducting audits on infrastructures to help identify risks and plan for their mitigation. While many of the infrastructures we spoke to had some form of auditing process, we found that audit processes could be better integrated into workflows, with the right support. 

In this workshop, we will first present our research findings, hear from UKRI DRI and from ‘audit experts’. We will then break into groups (in person and online) to discuss what should be included in audits for different infrastructures, how best to conduct them, and set priorities for implementation. 

Outputs from this workshop will feed into SSI’s work with UKRI DRI in developing new auditing practices.

The UKRI DRI programme team are keen to hear the views of the RSE community, and your early support in this session can help steer this process to the benefit of your work!

title: Developing the GOTO Telescope Control System
reasoning: This is a domain-specific software system built for astronomical observation (gravitational-wave optical transient detection), purpose-built for a particular scientific need.
abstract:
The Gravitational-wave Optical Transient Observer (GOTO) is an astronomical survey project utilising a network of robotic telescopes to monitor the night sky from two sites: La Palma in the Canary Islands and Siding Spring Observatory in Australia. The GOTO Telescope Control System (G‐TeCS) is a custom robotic control system, written predominantly in Python, which autonomously manages the telescope hardware and nightly operations, as well as directing the overall observing strategy of the network. Development of the control system begun prior to the commissioning of the first GOTO prototype on La Palma in 2017, and continued through the expansion of the La Palma site in 2021 and the addition of the Australian site in 2023.
At the sites, each telescope is automated by G-TeCS through a master control program (the “pilot”), which monitors and sends commands to the hardware daemons that interface with each part of the telescope hardware (cameras, mount, dome, etc). The pilot has robust systems for monitoring external conditions to ensure the safety of the telescopes in bad weather, as well as routines to attempt recovery of the hardware should any errors occur.
Also part of G-TeCS is the central alert monitoring and scheduling system, which is hosted at Warwick University in the UK. The G-TeCS “sentinel” listens to alert streams from different astrophysical detectors and processes any new alerts into targets for the GOTO telescopes. These are then sent out to the sites by the “scheduler” system, which also monitors the telescopes and determines what they should observe between alerts.
Here we will give a brief overview of the GOTO project and the G-TeCS software, focusing on the RSE involvement and outlining the future work planned over the next two years.

title: A Curated Collection of Software Quality Tools for Research: Insights from the EVERSE Technology Watch

abstract:
This work developed as part of the EVERSE - European Virtual Network for Research Software Excellence project, presents an initial curated collection of research software quality tools captured in the EVERSE Technology Watch. This includes a diverse set of research software quality tools, accompanied by key metadata outlining quality indicators and dimensions.These tools have been specifically selected to align with, adapt to, and extend the needs of various research communities, offering a comprehensive resource for improving software quality in research environments. Together with the EVERSE RSQKit, this collection aims to provide researchers and software engineers with an organised repository of information to evaluate and adopt tools to support and FAIRness within scientific research communities.
The ongoing development of this resource will continue to incorporate new tools and insights, supporting the evolving landscape of research software quality.

title: HPCRSE@RSECon25: 4th annual meeting of the HPC RSE community

abstract:
This event is organised by the HPC RSE Special Interest Group (SIG) to bring together the community of RSEs working in High Performance Computing (HPC) and Digital Research Infrastructure (DRI). The community covers a range of RSE roles from development of research software to support of HPC facilities, providing support to researchers. Our objectives are to provide peer support across the RSE HPC community, share experience and best practice, foster an open, self-sustaining community,  collaborate with other, associated communities and organisations and give the community an opportunity to steer the activities of the SIG.
The aims of the event are to share knowledge about the current “state-of-the-nation” in (UK) HPC, discuss topics of interest in the community, understand community priorities and needs and identify actions the SIG can take to address them. We aim to create a forum for network building and provide peer support to HPC RSEs: particularly those new to the HPC area and those working without support from a large RSE group.
The event is split into two sessions: technical and training/community. Each session starts with two short presentations for setting the scene, followed by a panel discussion. Presentations can consist of talks and/or live demos that demonstrate how HPC RSEs are supporting research excellence. Based on discussions in previous events, we have identified the following topics of particular interest, but the discussion will be driven by the attendees on the day (both online and in person). Technical topics: technological developments (e.g. new accelerator technology, exascale, new service), open source tools and libraries, environmental impact of HPC and HPC in TREs.  Training/community topics: training for RSEs, HPC RSE career progression/skills, community organisation and sustainability.

title: From demos to dependability: Practical evaluation strategies for AI applications
reasoning: This talk is about cross-cutting evaluation strategies for AI/LLM applications, applicable broadly to RSEs across domains. It's a software engineering practice talk, not domain-specific.
abstract:
The advent of Generative AI has transformed how we build AI models and software, but the speed we gain comes at a cost. Large language models (LLMs) let us add "intelligence" to an app in minutes, yet most prototypes stall before production because no one trusts their behaviour. We trace the shift from the traditional data-first, then model pipeline to today’s app-first, then API workflow and explain why it leaves teams blind, often without benchmark datasets or KPIs to judge performance.
The talk presents ways Research Software Engineers can close this gap by making evaluation a first-class citizen. We survey three families of evaluation for AI applications: manual prototypes, data-gathering tools, and synthetic benchmark generation, giving an overview of the field. We do a deep dive into the latest research and reflect on lessons learned over the past few years. To ground the theory, we walk through concrete examples from our own projects.
Attendees will leave with practical insights for matching evaluation strategy to project maturity, regulatory constraints, and available resources. Evaluation has become the critical bottleneck and RSEs are uniquely placed to turn it into an enabler for reproducible, sustainable science.

title: Geoscience SIG Inaugural Meeting: sharing knowledge and building bridges across the geoscience community.

abstract:
Following the successful Weather and Climate Birds of a Feather session at RSECon24, the Geoscience Special Interest Group (SIG) was formed, with over 100 RSEs signed up to our slack space. The geoscience RSE community consists of many RSEs working across the various fields of geoscience, spanning, among others, climate, weather, space science, geology and oceanography. 
In last year’s session, the needs and interests of this community were discussed. Those identified included a need for opportunities to share knowledge between organisations, break down silos and collaborate as well as interest in developing better guidance on career pathways.
As the inaugural hybrid meeting of the newly formed Geoscience SIG, we propose a BoF event to address these interests, aiming to build this community by bringing together RSEs from across the fields to network and facilitate knowledge exchange. This session is open to any RSEs working in or interested in geoscience and will feature keynotes from Bryan Lawrence (NCAS) & Andrea Sharpe (NERC), lightning talks on technical topics from within the community, breakout sessions to discuss community-driven topics (such as careers and building domain knowledge) and a session on the next steps for the SIG.

title: EBI Search: Engineering and Sustaining Metadata Infrastructure for Life Sciences
reasoning: This is about a search/metadata infrastructure purpose-built for life sciences (EMBL-EBI biological data). It's a domain-specific tool, fitting Research category, though it has heavy software engineering content.
abstract:
EBI Search indexes over 6.5 billion biological records across more than 170 datasets, providing the core metadata infrastructure behind EMBL-EBI’s discovery tools. It supports over 2.3 billion requests annually and enables unified search across biological data from both EMBL-EBI and external resources.
This poster presents an architectural overview of the EBI Search infrastructure and the engineering strategies used to sustain and evolve the system under increasing data volumes and user demands. These strategies include nightly parallel indexing pipelines, index partitioning to bypass Lucene's document limit, and API optimisations supporting faceted queries and bulk streaming across 2TB of data.
We explore how the team behind EBI Search balances competing requirements while maintaining an infrastructure with nearly two decades of continuous operation: optimising performance while ensuring reliability, expanding functionality without impacting backward compatibility, and delivering consistent performance across diverse data formats. 
Through this case study of EBI Search, we reflect on how targeted engineering decisions create lasting research infrastructure, connecting scientists with the data essential for breakthrough biological discoveries.

title: From Research Prototype to Real-World Impact with Nuvolos:  Reproducibility and Collaboration at Scale
reasoning: This describes a general-purpose cloud computational workspace platform serving RSEs across domains, focused on reproducibility, collaboration, and infrastructure management.
abstract:
RSEs work at the intersection of research and software engineering, combining domain expertise with technical skill to deliver reproducible science. But too much of that time is swallowed by fixing broken dependencies, rebuilding environments for each project, and keeping infrastructure running. Nuvolos takes on the heavy computational lifting, provisioning, scaling, and managing compute, so RSEs can focus on the science itself.
Nuvolos is a seamlessly integrated, powerful, and collaborative cloud‑based computational workspace. It removes operational friction, simplifies software setup, and ensures computational environments are instantly available,  anywhere, through a browser.
Designed with the evolving needs of the RSE community in mind, Nuvolos reflects shared values that drive sustainable, high‑impact research:
Empowerment – Instant access to tools like Python, R, Julia, MATLAB, Stata, any IDE, backed by scalable CPU & GPU compute.
Reproducibility & Rigor – Full versioning ensures every experiment can be trusted, verified, and built upon.
Collaboration & Accessibility – Seamless teamwork across institutions with shared, browser‑based access to computational resources.
Sustainability & Reusability – Maintainable code, reusable workflows, and preserved datasets extend research impact beyond a single project.
Community Contribution – Support for open science practices, helping RSEs share tools, methods, and results with the wider community.
Innovation & Agility – Continuous integration of the latest frameworks, from TensorFlow and PyTorch to AlphaFold,  keeps research on the cutting edge.
Simplicity & Control – Backend complexity is managed for you, while you retain full control over projects and environments.
Nuvolos is more than a platform. It is a partner in advancing science that is sustainable, reproducible, and openly shared, helping the RSE community work more productively, collaboratively, and with lasting impact.

title: How to build a project team: experiences from the Turing
reasoning: Talk about managing and staffing RSE teams at the Turing Institute, focused on people and team organization rather than tools or specific research.
abstract:
Research Software Engineers can be asked to work on a very wide range of projects. These project vary in many different ways, such as the number of people involved, the duration, whether they are fully internal to an organisation or working with external partners, or how much they are shaped by the RSEs. The requirements for RSEs can vary significantly too, meaning that identifying the optimum team for any given project can be challenging.
The Research Engineering Group at the Alan Turing Institute has approximately 40 people with a range of different skills (RSEs, Research Data Scientists, Research Computer Engineers, Data Wranglers). As a team we provide software engineering expertise to many of the projects that the Turing is working on. Over the past 5 years, there have been several changes in how we work. The team has grown significantly in size, and the Turing has gone through a transition from most projects being stand-alone to a mission based vision with a stronger focus on effective real-world impact. In the earlier phase, REG members would typically work on a couple of projects at a time, and they would change at least one of these projects relatively frequently. Under the new setup, team members typically only work on one mission at a time, often for much longer time periods.
This transition has created many opportunities, but also some challenges in how we work both as a team and individually. In this talk, we consider some of the lessons learned from this transition, and  how they can be applied to RSE teams more generally when staffing projects.

title: Loome: Empowering research teams with scalable, secure cloud resources

Run in collaboration with our colleagues in the Data Analytics team it provided research active staff with access to up to six months of RSE expertise. title: flowR: Program Slicing and Dependency Analysis to Improve the Reuse of R Scripts
reasoning: flowR is a general-purpose program slicer/dataflow analyzer for R scripts, applicable across domains to improve reproducibility and reuse — a cross-cutting tool for RSEs.
abstract:
A program slicer reduces a program to only the parts relevant to a certain variable of interest like a visualization or a statistical test. This way, a slice is usually a much smaller script that is easier to understand, has fewer dependencies, and focuses only on the analysis of interest.Such slices can be beneficial for both reviewers, trying to understand and validate the methodology, and authors wishing to reuse and reproduce existing analyses. Even if the original script is not executable due to missing dependencies, a slice that does not rely on them can be executed and reused independently.In our talk, we introduce flowR, a novel program slicer and dataflow analyzer for R, alongside its Visual Studio Code extension and RStudio addin which allow users to interactively slice their scripts directly from their IDE.To calculate slices and the dependency information, flowR uses a pipeline architecture that first parses the R code into an abstract syntax tree, which is subsequently normalized into a version-independent intermediate representation.Based on this representation, flowR uses an interprocedural dataflow analysis to construct a static dataflow graph of the entire script.This graph describes the dependencies of variables and function calls, compensating for the inherently dynamic nature of R.A program slice is essentially the subgraph that is reachable from the variable of interest.
Besides slicing, we also provide a dependency view of the entire analysis script which shows the inputs, sourced files, required libraries, and produced outputs to help users find and understand the important parts and required inputs.

title: Causal AI: Evaluating AI Workflows on HPC Environments Using Causal Testing
reasoning: An open-source, general-purpose testing tool for AI/ML workflows on HPC — a cross-cutting technique applicable across domains, not tied to a specific scientific question.
abstract:
As AI and machine learning become central to scientific research, the ability to rigorously verify their behaviour has struggled to keep up. Traditional software testing breaks down in this context: scientific pipelines rarely have a single correct output to test against, their configuration spaces are vast, and their stochastic nature makes it difficult to distinguish genuine errors from expected variation. The consequence is that many scientific AI systems are deployed with limited understanding of what actually drives their outputs.
Causal testing offers a principled alternative. By encoding domain knowledge as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) - a structured representation of the cause-and-effect relationships between variables, such as batch size or floating point precision - researchers can formally test whether their pipeline behaves as expected, using data already collected from prior runs. This removes the need for expensive re-experimentation and makes verification tractable even at HPC scale.
This poster presents causal-ai, an open-source tool developed as part of the N8 CIR AI4Science project to improve the ability of evaluating complex AI/ML workflows on HPC systems. The tool provides direct HPC integration, a command-line interface, and worked case studies across image classification and video domain adaptation pipelines. Cross-cluster comparisons further reveal platform-dependent effects that conventional evaluation metrics do not capture.

title: Kill your shell scripts: Reproducible workflow management with Snakemake
reasoning: Snakemake is a general-purpose workflow management tool applicable across domains, focusing on reproducibility and automation practices for RSEs broadly.
abstract:
You have a process to automate. It only has a couple of steps, one after the other, so you write a shell script. Then, you add more steps. Perhaps you want to cache some of the intermediary state, and only re-run when the underlying data change, to save time. And maybe what final stage you run depends on what output you’re looking for. Before long, you’re either writing a rat’s nest of ad-hoc code looking after these edge cases, or writing your own domain-specific language within Bash to handle this task of… Workflow Management.
It turns out that you are far from the first person to have encountered the problem of workflow management, and there are many mature tools available to reduce your maintenance burden and let you focus on your specific workflows of interest. In this walkthrough I’ll introduce how to use Snakemake, a workflow manager developed in life science and commonly used in particle physics, but applicable for many purposes more widely. Topics I’ll cover include how to define rules that depend on the output of other rules, templated rules that can work for a variety of input files, and rules depending on some external metadata or configuration; how to parallelise running a workflow on a single machine; and how to run steps of a workflow using external computing resources such as an HPC cluster.

title: Coding Confessions: Normalising Failure in Research Software
reasoning: Focuses on RSE mental health, imposter syndrome, and community discussion about failures — a profession/people-focused session.
abstract:
What?
At Coding Confessions RSEs talk openly about mistakes they've made developing software, running systems or managing projects. First developed during the SSI’s Collaborations Workshop Hackday 2021, Coding Confessions panels took place at RSECon 2021, 2022 and 2023. This year we are broadening the scope to provide a wider discussion and cover some of the commonly recurring themes including imposter syndrome, visibility of hidden roles, AI going wrong and management of junior staff.
Why?
Mental health is an important issue for RSEs (34% of RSEs have experienced a mental health condition since becoming RSEs - 2022 RSE Mental Health Survey). RSEs should work in environments where they can freely discuss their mistakes, yet often lack confidence when publishing or submitting their code for review or asking for help navigating other challenges. Common reasons for this include my code “isn’t good enough or isn’t complete enough”, alongside wider professional anxieties such as “I should know this”, “I can’t ask for help”, or “I don’t belong here”. We encourage people to share their insecurities to normalise talking about mistakes and knowledge gaps.
How?
“Traditional” Coding Confessions events (as run 2021-2023) consisted of a panel where several RSEs talked about mistakes they've made in software they've developed. This year we will be expanding to a broader discussion. We will begin with a traditional coding confessions panel followed by some short talks and a group discussion. We will publish blog posts with OLS, SSI or ConveRSE to disseminate the findings of this session.

title: Where does the rigor go? Research software and the future of trustworthy science.
reasoning: This is a keynote-style talk about the RSE profession's future role in ensuring trustworthy science amid AI, drawing on funder/editor/community perspectives. It's about people, profession, and cross-cutting practice rather than a specific tool or domain.
abstract: Generative AI now makes it dramatically easier to produce something that looks like research: analysis code, figures, literature reviews, even whole papers. The mechanisms research relies on to establish trust were built for a slower, human-paced enterprise, and they are struggling with the volume. Software got here first: this community has a two-year head start on questions the rest of research is only beginning to ask, and RSE work is already changing shape, away from writing code for researchers and toward specification, verification, and the judgment that makes AI-assisted work trustworthy. I'll share observations from my perspectives as a funder, a journal editor, and a long-time member of this community and offer some thoughts on where research software engineering goes next.

title: Green RSE Special Interest Group: Building a Environmental Skills and Knowledge in the RSE Community.
reasoning: This is about a Special Interest Group building community around green/sustainability skills within the RSE profession, including career frameworks and training pathways - clearly Community focused, with sustainability tooling as a secondary theme.
abstract:
There is an urgent need to reduce the environmental impact of research computing. While many research institutions have high-level commitments to emissions reductions, it is not always clear how these will be achieved. The UKRI DRI Net Zero scoping report found that in many cases this transition is hindered not by a lack of knowledge, but by insufficient knowledge-sharing and structures to enable behaviour change.
RSEs are well placed to help drive this transition - both through their technical skills and by acting as agents of knowledge exchange across research communities. Despite this, environmental sustainability is seldom an official part of the RSE roles.
The Green RSE Special Interest Group (https://socrse.github.io/green-sig/) is working to change this by building a supportive community that helps RSEs play an active role in the transition to sustainable research computing. In this submission, we reflect on two years of progress, including: defining what environmental sustainability means within the RSE role; identifying best practices for environmentally responsible software; and developing resources to improve code efficiency and reduce energy usage.
Looking ahead, we argue that realising the potential of RSEs as sustainability champions will require formal recognition of green skills within RSE career frameworks, dedicated training pathways, and stronger institutional mandates that make sustainability a core part of RSE roles. The Green RSE SIG is committed to building the community and resources to make this possible.

title: Using Causal Reasoning to Test Scientific Software
reasoning: Talk is about a general-purpose testing technique/framework (Causal Testing Framework) applicable across scientific software domains, not tied to one discipline.
abstract:
From predicting the weather to simulating disease transmission, scientific software plays an increasingly pivotal role in developing scientific understanding that informs our everyday lives. However, they are also some of the most difficult software systems to properly test. Because the developers are often the scientists themselves, they may not be familiar with established testing techniques and are likely to focus on scientific results rather than software quality. From a technical standpoint, scientific software systems tend to exhibit several characteristics that make traditional testing techniques impractical and often insufficient. They have large, complex input spaces, are computationally expensive to run, often rely on stochastic black-box components, and are applied in exploratory contexts where the expected outcomes are not known. 
Causality-driven testing has recently emerged as a potential solution to these challenges. Building on the concept of metamorphic testing — investigating whether a change to the input configuration yields the expected corresponding change in output — causal testing employs domain knowledge and existing runtime data to efficiently use the limited test runs that can be performed. In this walkthrough, we will use real examples to demonstrate the limitations of traditional unit testing. We will then show how metamorphic testing can go beyond these limitations, how causal reasoning can be employed to increase the efficiency of the testing process, and how the Causal Testing Framework can automate much of this.

title: Geoscience RSE SIG Annual Meeting: Challenges and Opportunities of RSE Careers in Geosciences

Yet opportunities to connect across these areas remain limited. It will showcase community highlights through short lightning talks and a keynote by Nick Jefferson (University of Leeds) on the development of the African nowcasting mobile phone app FASTA, alongside a panel discussion exploring the varied career pathways available to geoscience RSEs across academia, government institutes, and the private sector.

title: From Fragmented Tools to FAIR Research Infrastructure in Biologics Discovery
reasoning: The talk describes software infrastructure built specifically for biologics discovery (antibody cloning, DNA ordering) — a domain-specific research workflow, though it also highlights general RSE practices and FAIR principles.
abstract:
High-throughput biologics discovery workflows frequently depend on fragmented tools, manual coordination, and disconnected laboratory and computational systems. As scientific programmes scale across multiple research sites, these workflows can become operational bottlenecks that limit reproducibility, traceability, and data reuse.
This talk presents how Research Software Engineers collaborated with scientists to transform antibody cloning and DNA ordering workflows into scalable research infrastructure supporting distributed biologics discovery operations across UK and US sites. By integrating multiple external services through automated API-driven workflows, the platform reduced complex manual processes involving repeated file downloads, uploads, and over 50 user interactions into streamlined workflows requiring fewer than five clicks and no manual file handling.
The system incorporates asynchronous task orchestration using Redis and Celery, Single Sign-On integration, CI/CD pipelines with GitHub Actions, and automated metadata validation to support reliable high-throughput operations.
Beyond operational efficiency, the work demonstrates how RSE practices can improve FAIR data quality and enable AI-ready research workflows through richer metadata capture, improved traceability, and standardised process integration. The talk will discuss lessons learned from embedding software engineering practices into rapidly evolving scientific environments while balancing flexibility, usability, and reproducibility.

title: A Community-Owned Database Mapping dRTP Roles, Skills, and Training
reasoning: This is about mapping RSE roles, skills, and training - clearly about the profession and community development, not a specific tool or research domain.
abstract:
As is typical of all digital Research Technical Professionals (dRTPs), Research Software Engineer is a role that encompasses a wide variety of potential competencies and areas of work. Individual RSEs practice a range of skills, often specialising in a particular research domain and/or set of techniques/technologies. 
With increasing professionalisation, a need has grown for this diversity to be documented and mapped. Among other things, a mapping of skills to roles and training provision could facilitate the professional development of individual RSEs, the management of RSE teams, and research into the RSE community at large.
Several recent initiatives have contributed to the mapping of the dRTP skills and training landscape. The community is making unprecedented progress in defining the knowledge, skills, and abilities required for growth in a dRTP career. However, the concurrency of these different initiatives presents a challenge to the community: how can we avoid the simultaneous development of multiple competing standards to describe these things?
This poster introduces a database, developed and maintained by the newly-formed dRTP Landscape Mapping Coordination Group, that describes the roles performed by dRTPs, the skills they need to succeed in those roles, and the training available to equip them with those skills. This builds on the work of many recent initiatives, drawing together previously disparate outputs.
We will describe our collaborative approach to developing the database, explain how community members can interact with it and why they might want to, and discuss our strategy to avoid the “XKCD 927” problem (https://xkcd.com/927/).

title: MetSTAC: Building STAC Catalogs for Machine‑Learning‑Ready Data
reasoning: MetSTAC is built for meteorological/climate ML data at the Met Office, but the approach and tool are cross-cutting metadata infrastructure applicable to any data-intensive domain, centering on FAIR principles and STAC standards.
abstract:
Machine learning workflows depend on access to large and well described datasets, yet locating these datasets remains a significant barrier to development. Whilst we have the tools required to build these datasets, they are often forgotten or lost, leading to duplicated effort. Within the Met Office, data used for machine learning spans multiple storage systems and formats, making discovery and reuse difficult.
The ML Datasets team has adopted the SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC) standard as a common metadata layer for machine learning ready meteorological and climate data. This poster presents MetSTAC, a Python library developed to generate STAC catalogs for complex scientific datasets without requiring data duplication or format changes.
We show how MetSTAC supports automated metadata extraction and template driven catalog generation for both gridded NetCDF data and cloud optimised Zarr stores. The poster demonstrates how STAC catalogs provide a single, discoverable view of datasets distributed across local and cloud platforms, enabling users to search and assess data suitability quickly and easily.
By aligning with FAIR data principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) MetSTAC illustrates the role of research software engineering in building sustainable metadata infrastructure. While developed in a meteorological context, the approaches demonstrated are applicable to other data intensive scientific domains facing similar discovery and reuse challenges.

title: Cloud Cybersecurity for Research Engineers
reasoning: Cross-cutting best practices for cloud cybersecurity applicable to RSEs broadly, not tied to a specific research domain despite the patient data example.
abstract:
The availability of large datasets and breakthroughs in machine learning have had a profound impact on how modern science is conducted. Once the preserve of computer science, large-scale compute has become a universal requirement across research fields from astrophysics to zoology. This has created a huge demand for computing infrastructure within research institutions, where academics often compete for scarce resources. 
Cloud computing offers a viable alternative. Cloud platforms such as Azure, Google Cloud and AWS offer researchers abundant pay-as-you-go computing resources at competitive prices, without the need to buy hardware or manage software. This flexibility is welcome, but comes with the caveat that operating in the public cloud means working on the open internet without professional IT support. Without appropriate measures, conducting scientific research on the internet exposes researchers and their institutions to security threats that, in the worst-case, could end in sensitive data leaks and ICO fines. 
In this walkthrough, we will showcase best practices for performing research on the public cloud securely, using a motivating example of patient data analysis performed on Azure. We will cover: 
Improving user authentication with 2FA and password protocols.
Protecting your virtual network using a firewall.
Using a remote desktop gateway for accessing virtual machines securely.
Limiting access to protect cloud storage.
Using secrets for managing and sharing sensitive information.
Monitoring cloud resources for threat detection.

title: From Antibody Clones to DNA Order: RSEs Streamlining Biologics Discovery
reasoning: This is about software built for a specific domain (antibody cloning/biologics discovery), a domain-specific workflow automation. Cannot be explained without naming the discipline.
abstract:
High-throughput biologics discovery workflows often rely on fragmented tools, ad hoc processes, and manual data handling across laboratory and computational systems. As antibody cloning projects scale, these disconnected workflows can introduce bottlenecks, increase the risk of human error, and make reproducibility and traceability difficult to maintain.
This poster presents how Research Software Engineers collaborated with scientists to streamline high-throughput antibody cloning and DNA ordering workflows within a biologics discovery pipeline. The work focused on automating sequence processing, metadata validation, construct tracking, and DNA order generation, reducing manual intervention while improving consistency across experiments.
The project demonstrates how RSE practices can support the research journey by transforming evolving laboratory processes into scalable and maintainable research infrastructure. The poster will showcase the transition from fragmented workflows toward an automated pipeline designed to support reproducibility, auditability, and efficient collaboration between computational and laboratory teams.
Attendees will gain insight into practical approaches for workflow automation in research environments where scientific and software processes intersect, alongside lessons learned from balancing flexibility, usability, and software quality in a rapidly evolving discovery setting.

title: Automatic Transcription: Building a Safe, On-Premises Service for Sensitive Research Data
reasoning: Scriber is a general-purpose transcription service applicable across qualitative research domains, focusing on software engineering, deployment, and institutional integration rather than a specific scientific question. Strong community/institutional translation angle as secondary.
abstract:
Automatic transcription has become essential to qualitative research, but mainstream commercial services rely on cloud pipelines unsuitable for recordings covered by institutional information governance. Without sanctioned alternatives, researchers default to consumer tools and universities absorb the risk.
This talk describes how the University of Sheffield moved from a recurring pattern of unresolvable support tickets to delivering Scriber: an open-source, on-premises transcription service that processes sensitive audio and video without data leaving institutional infrastructure.
We follow the full journey: scoping researcher needs; navigating Information Security and Data Protection Office assessments; securing prioritisation in the IT Services delivery plan; prototyping and user-testing with qualitative researchers; writing end-user documentation; integrating with the IT Support Helpdesk so researchers have a recognised route when something goes wrong; and scaling horizontally across virtual machines.
The architectural commitment that made this possible was integrating directly with the existing Research Storage service: researchers deposit files in their usual storage and collect transcripts there. No web application, no separate data store, no data movement outside sanctioned systems. Scriber orchestrates OpenAI Whisper via rootless Docker containers as a background systemd service on a university-managed virtual server. Researchers drop a file into a folder and collect a transcript — no new accounts, no cloud, no specialist knowledge required.
The central argument is that delivering Scriber was an act of institutional translation, not solely software development. It exercises the research-understanding strand of the RSE career path alongside the technical. Scriber is open source; attendees are encouraged to adapt it for their own institutions.

title: Research Software Engineering and Fault-tolerant Quantum Computing
reasoning: This talk is about how software engineering (including RSE) is applied to build quantum computers at a specific company, focusing on a specific domain (quantum computing hardware/software). It's domain-specific research software, though it also touches on RSE career accessibility.
abstract: Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) is a full-stack quantum hardware and software company employing a diversity of skillsets to build quantum computers from the ground up and deploy them into data centres around the world. Quantum computing is often viewed as an esoteric, highly specialised field where a PhD in Quantum Computing is an entry requirement. In this talk we will explore how OQC leverages traditional software engineering skills, including research software engineering, to build the next generation of fault-tolerant quantum computers the world will depend on. I hope to convince you that quantum computing is an accessible field for RSEs and highlight the opportunities which will push the quantum revolution forward.

title: A pitch for sustainable career pathways for digital research technical professionals (dRTPs)
reasoning: This is about career pathways, retention, and professional development for RSEs/dRTPs at a university—clearly about people and the profession.
abstract: The growth of the Advanced Research Computing team at the University of Birmingham from ten to over forty members over a period of eight years illustrates the value provided to the University’s research, particularly as research grants have directly funded much of this growth. However, these highly skilled staff have suffered from unclear or time-consuming pathways to advance their careers, through ad-hoc regrading or by applying for new posts at a more senior level. As a result, only 32% of Advanced Research Computing respondents in a recent survey “understand how the university can support their career aspirations,” and this uncertainty leads to costly turnover. As a result, we developed and presented a business case recommending a career framework and promotion pathway to IT Services leadership. In this pitch, we justify our recommendation by outlining how reduced retention of dRTPs compromises the University’s research strategy. We also provide an outline of the finance implications and risks of implementing the scheme and how we plan to mitigate them. While developing the pitch, we identified common themes and risks through discussions with dRTPs across different universities. In this poster, we will describe our business case as a blueprint on how to find common ground between dRTPs’ career aspirations and the University’s priorities and HR and finance concerns. By sharing our ideas, successes, and failures, we hope to share strategies with the community on persuading higher education institutions to make dRTP roles more sustainable, fulfilling, long-term careers.

title: PyEarthTools: Accelerating the use of machine learning for reproducible environmental science
reasoning: PyEarthTools is a domain-specific tool built for environmental science ML pipelines, tied to that discipline's data patterns.
abstract: Machine learning opens up many new opportunities in environmental science, through discovering new insights from data to reduced costs of simulation. However a lot of environmental data does not work “out the box” with standard machine learning tools. As a result researchers need to spend a lot of effort into custom data pipelines for each problem. As the field has matured common usage patterns have emerged. PyEarthTools aims to provide common functionality for the use of ML in environmental science research that enables researchers to quickly build shareable, reproducible ML pipelines for training and inference that can run on many different platforms. A key focus is on enabling common patterns of data access and transformation required for ML. We will demonstrate how a domain specific tool that implements common domain patterns in data and functionality can greatly accelerate research and make it easier to follow FAIR principles. In encapsulating expert knowledge into components and pipelines, this can also make it easier for data scientists and experts from other domains to incorporate environmental science data into their work.

title: Building a Reproducibility Check Service for Computational Research
reasoning: This talk describes an institutional service/initiative for reproducibility checks across research outputs, focusing on cross-cutting reproducibility practice and RSE team implementation recommendations. It's about a profession-wide/institutional initiative rather than a specific tool or scientific domain.
abstract:
Reproducibility remains a persistent challenge in computational research, despite increasing requirements from journals for authors to share underlying software and data. While such policies are a step forward, they do not guarantee that published results can be independently reproduced.
In this talk, we present the Reproducibility Check initiative, developed by the TU Delft Digital Competence Center (DCC) in collaboration with 4TU.ResearchData repository. The initiative targets TU Delft researchers who deposit the software and data underlying their publications in 4TU.ResearchData. Deposits are screened and authors are invited to participate in a reproducibility check, in which RSEs from the DCC attempt to reproduce the published results using the CODECHECK process (Nüst and Eglen, 2021).
We will share insights from the pilot phase, running since spring 2025, highlighting common challenges and strategies to address them, including approaches to engaging researchers and lowering participation barriers. Based on these experiences, we provide recommendations for institutions and RSE teams interested in implementing similar initiatives.

title: From reinventing the wheel to building bicycles
reasoning: This is about mapping DRI-funded skills/people initiatives across research councils to foster collaboration—clearly about the profession, funding landscape, and community coordination rather than a specific tool or research domain.
abstract: There has been a lot of investment in skills and people through a number of DRI initiatives in recent years, across multiple research councils. As a result there have been a number of ovelapping proposals funded either simultaneously or immediately proceeding each other, often with limited visibility of each other. The aim of which is to share lessons learnt and spark collaboration to move forward together more efficiently than working independently. The poster will be a visual representation of the projects and synergies identified.

title: Porting GLASS to the Python Array API: A Clear View to GPU Portability.
reasoning: GLASS is a cosmology-specific library for galaxy surveys, so the work is tied to a research domain, though the talk emphasizes general porting techniques (Array API, GPU portability) applicable more broadly.
abstract: GLASS is a Python library designed to generate full-universe cosmological simulations for large-scale galaxy surveys. Historically, the use of NumPy has been essential to GLASS’ success, allowing rapid development and integration with a wide range of existing cosmological software. However, as simulation demands grow and high-performance computing shifts towards GPU-heavy architectures, GLASS must evolve to support these workloads. As NumPy was not designed for non-CPU devices, it now poses a significant bottleneck to this evolution. To overcome this, we are porting GLASS to the Python Array API, decoupling the library from NumPy and enabling native GPU execution. By adopting this standard, we are expanding GLASS to support all Array API-compliant libraries, broadening its ecosystem and utility. This transition involves managing varying levels of Array API maturity across libraries and optimising core scientific models for GPU parallelism. The resulting GPU-enabled GLASS provides a significant performance boost whilst remaining performant on CPUs, facilitating seamless integration with GPU-native workflows, and enabling advanced techniques like auto-differentiable simulations via JAX.

title: Accelerating Machine Learning Research in Fusion Through a Pydantic‑Centred Human‑in‑the‑Loop Architecture
reasoning: The talk describes a domain-specific annotation platform (TokTagger) built for nuclear fusion tokamak diagnostic data, purpose-built for a specific scientific need. While it uses general tools (Pydantic, Ray, MongoDB), the artifact is clearly tied to fusion research.
abstract:
Training high-performing ML models requires large volumes of high quality, labelled data. While nuclear fusion experiments generate extensive datasets – JET produced 105,929 pulses, each with more than 10GB of raw data [1] – much of this data lacks the annotations necessary for effective ML training. Retrospective annotation is both challenging and time consuming, as domain experts lack the appropriate tools to effectively label historic pulses.
To address this challenge, RSEs and domain experts have collaborated to develop an open-source human-in-the-loop annotation platform for labelling tokamak diagnostic data [2]. This combines a web-based user interface and a REST API built around data models defined using Pydantic [3], with validated annotations stored in a MongoDB [4] database for later reuse. The modular design supports multiple data access layers from different machines, with simple integration of new sources.
Custom ML models can be defined by the user, with training and prediction tasks scheduled via the UI and executed using Ray [5]. These reduce the workload for scientists, who can focus on refining model predictions rather than labelling from scratch. This demonstrates how infrastructure co-developed between RSEs and domain experts, focussed on data validation, extensibility and reusability, plays a key role in the research journey.
[1]: Vega, J., et al. "New developments at JET in diagnostics, real-time control, data acquisition and information retrieval with potential application to ITER." Fusion Engineering and Design 84.12 (2009): 2136-2144. 
[2]: TokTagger. https://github.com/ukaea/toktagger 
[3]: Pydantic. https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic
[4]: The MongoDB Database. https://github.com/mongodb/mongo
[5]: Ray. https://github.com/ray-project/ray

title: From Model to Scenario Engine: A Reproducible ABM for UK Net Zero Analysis
reasoning: The talk centers on transforming an ABM for UK Net Zero policy analysis - a specific domain application - though it also emphasizes general software engineering practices for stochastic ABMs that could apply broadly.
abstract:
Agent-based modelling (ABMs) has increasingly been used to study socio-economic transitions. These computational models feature heterogeneous agents, decision-making, and feedback effects that are difficult to capture in aggregate models. Yet, these features that make ABMs valuable also make them hard to reproduce and evaluate as research software, especially when stochastic behaviour is involved. 
In this talk, we share the software engineering effort to transform a baseline ABM for macroeconomic analysis into a tool for comparing UK Net Zero policy intervention scenarios. The methodology combines design choices, including:
Coding economic shocks targeting different economic markets
A UK-specific data pipeline
Monte Carlo simulation (MC)
Reproducibility controls
Visualisation dashboards
Simulation-based inference (SBI)
We show that a more straightforward separation of the main logic from scenario interventions in the code makes it easier to test, maintain, and extend with new economic behaviours. We also explain scenario uncertainty with MC and SBI. Finally, we discuss how dashboards make outputs easier to inspect and compare for both technical and non-technical audiences.
Although the work is motivated by UK Net Zero policy analysis, the broader contribution is a dialogue of software engineering practices for making large-scale stochastic ABMs more credible and reusable as research software. The talk will be relevant to anyone working on computational models where scientific value depends as much on implementation rigour as on the underlying theory. In addition to making the ABM applicable to policy analysis, we argue that the design choices improve the model's implementation, enabling better software quality assessments.

title: FORGE: tackling four decades of technical debt in an operational forecasting system
reasoning: The talk centers on modernizing ECMWF's forecasting system (weather/climate domain-specific software), but the focus is on cross-cutting RSE practices: testing strategies, CI/CD, open-sourcing, and technical debt management. Since it's explicitly framed as a case study for the RSE community with generalizable lessons, Software leads, but the domain-specific nature makes Research a strong secondary.
abstract:
ECMWF's Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) has been in continuous development since the 1980s. It runs operationally every few hours, drives medium-range forecasts used across Europe, and underpins climate reanalyses and emerging hybrid AI–physics models. It also carries four decades of technical debt, must adapt to GPU-accelerated and external HPC platforms, and is being progressively open-sourced. 
FORGE — Forecast System Regeneration — is a medium-term programme to modernise this codebase: tackling the technical debt, refactoring model and data structures, improving the supporting software stack, and easing deployment beyond ECMWF.
This talk gives an overview of FORGE and uses it as a case study, focusing on two strands of possible interest to the RSE community: (1) a layered testing strategy spanning unit tests, integration tests, and CI on full forecast experiments — with a planned end-to-end clone of the operational suite as the basis for continuous deployment; and (2) the open-sourcing of operational forecasting software, supported by governance improvements: clearer code ownership, review processes, automated linting, and joint development with our Member States.
We share what we've learned so far. Persuading the organisation that technical debt was worth addressing was a significant step. Finding time for debt work amid pressure to deliver new science remains hard, and the debt itself makes things slower. We are experimenting with agentic AI code-generation for behaviour-preserving refactoring as something that might help — using the test harness as the safety net that makes faster, more automated cleanup possible.
A companion talk by Kipling et al. covers FORGE's workflow-orchestration strand.

title: Detecting novel biothreats from global news with AI – from research to production deployment in the Cabinet Office National Situation Centre
reasoning: The talk centers on a domain-specific tool (Biothreat Media Analyser) built for biothreat detection, but emphasizes generalizable patterns for productionising AI research. It's a case study of a specific application, making it Research, with Software as secondary due to the transferable engineering lessons.
abstract:
The National Situation Centre (SitCen), part of Cabinet Office Briefing Rooms (COBR), are responsible for alerting government to potential new biothreats as soon as they emerge. Worldwide news stories are a vital signal for early stage novel disease detection, however the volume of data makes manual review impossible.

In this talk, we will present Biothreat Media Analyser (BMA), a collaboration between STFC Hartree Centre and SitCen which uses frontier embedding models to continuously analyse news stories from around the world, flagging potentially novel biothreats. This collaboration involved RSEs, data scientists, and data engineers from STFC and SitCen. We will discuss the journey of this project from initial ideation and investigation through research and exploration all the way to implementation, iteration, and production deployment.

We will tell the story of this project and the critical role that RSEs played from start to finish. We will cover:
The project journey, from ideation to production.
The ongoing collaborative two-way relationship between the data scientists doing the research and the RSEs turning it into production code.
Architectural decisions necessary to adapt the research from notebooks analysing static data to algorithms running continuously on live data, including the associated trade-offs.
Lessons from delivering research software into a high-impact, high-stakes, information-sensitive government department.
We aim to give attendees concrete patterns for productionising AI research and an understand of what it takes to turn research into operationally trustworthy production infrastructure used in critical decision-making.

title: HPCRSE@RSECon26: 5th annual meeting of the HPC RSE community
